summary:
Huancavelica stands under Peru's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct has not been an offence since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity itself is not criminalised, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. What a trans visitor to Huancavelica faces is the national position, because the region has no recorded trans-specific law, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident of its own: statutory restriction of public-facility access, no hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and rising recorded violence.

Peru's Congress has legislated directly against trans people's use of public facilities. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved and exempted from a second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject to narrow listed exceptions covering custody, situations requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The Women and Family Commission had unanimously approved the merged dictamen on 20 February 2025, and the package also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage, including inclusive wording such as 'women in their diversity'.

The stated justification for the restriction is the prevention of child sexual abuse. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers. UN reporting cited in the same analysis shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

The legislative trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho, who co-authored the July 2024 violence report, calls the measure discriminatory and warns that bathroom access would come to depend on the personal judgment of security staff, including identity checks, noting that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The bill was still at committee stage as of February 2025 in the sources available here.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised such discrimination from 7 January 2017 through articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, but Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Recorded violence is rising and understated. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru in 2020–2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), ahead of 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty such as multiple gunshots and stabbings; the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias filed in 2020. Co-author Gianna Camacho states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One 2023 case illustrates the pattern: in February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.
tangentialFactors:
Facility restriction is national in scope but its enforcement sits with private security and staff discretion rather than a published Huancavelica protocol. Gianna Camacho's warning that access would turn on individual judgment, including ID checks, indicates that a trans visitor's experience in any Peruvian facility, in Huancavelica as elsewhere, depends on how a given guard reads documents and presentation.

The RESTRICTION's stated child-protection rationale is contested on the evidence. UN reporting cited by IDEHPUCP finds trans people are more often victims than aggressors of violence, and no record exists of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms; the absence of a documented predicate for the rule is a point of open legal and political dispute rather than settled fact.

The national violence statistics that frame the Huancavelica assessment are concentrated in Lima and its district of Carabayllo, and the sex-work exposure figure comes from Lima and Callao. No regional breakdown of the 54 murders or the 170 violation cases is available here, so the national totals cannot be read as a measure of risk specific to Huancavelica.

Legal recognition of gender is partial nationally: transgender Peruvians may change their legal name, and a Constitutional Court ruling of 21 October 2016, published 8 November, permits gender change on national identity documents through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery, reversing a 2014 bar. A Gender Identity Law introduced on 4 November 2016 remained pending as of March 2021. A visitor's documents therefore reflect whatever judicial process they completed at home.

Adjacent national turbulence affects how protections are framed: the April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs permits registration revocation on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being used against queer organising, and a Lima constitutional court struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist challenge.
localsOnly:
Residents of Huancavelica are subject to the same national facility statute as visitors. Article 5 bars entry to any public sanitary service that does not correspond to a person's 'biological sex', with exceptions limited to custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The bill was approved by the congressional plenary on 2 April 2025, having cleared the Women and Family Commission unanimously on 20 February 2025 as a merged dictamen of bills presented by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante.

The same package prohibits 'ambiguous' bathroom signage, which the sources describe as reaching inclusive wording such as 'women in their diversity'. Establishments in Huancavelica that carry such signage face a national prohibition, though no regional enforcement instruction is recorded in the sources available here.

The path to legal recognition is judicial. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity, and since the Constitutional Court's ruling of 21 October 2016, published 8 November 2016, gender markers on national identity documents may be changed through a court process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change and matching passports and identity documents was introduced on 4 November 2016 and was still pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classification has shifted. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for insurance classification, and health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance in the same month. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

Reporting channels exist at national level for the violence recorded by the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI, which logged 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023 including state violence and incitement to discrimination. Whether Huancavelica has its own receiving body or documented caseload is not stated in the sources here.
outOfScopeNotes:
The bill numbering for the restroom legislation is unresolved across sources: the inventory for this record cites bills 6506 and 8457, while the parent-framework material cites 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR. The discrepancy has not been reconciled against the Congressional records.

The legislative status of the restroom restriction is described unevenly. One source places the merged dictamen at committee stage as of February 2025 and another records plenary approval with exemption from a second vote on 2 April 2025; whether the text was subsequently enacted, published and in force is not confirmed by any source in this inventory.

No Huancavelica-specific data exists in any source here: no regional ordinance, no enforcement record, no reported incident, no local facility guidance, and no regional breakdown of the 54 murders or 170 violation cases recorded nationally for 2020–2023. The regional assessment therefore rests entirely on the national framework.

Enforcement practice in Huancavelica under the facility statute is not sourced. The only evidence on how the rule operates day to day is Gianna Camacho's warning about security-staff discretion and identity checks, which is a prediction rather than a documented regional practice.

The claim that Huancavelica has no trans-specific local law is an absence-of-record finding drawn from the sources supplied, not a verified survey of all municipal and regional enactments in the department.
